abstract: A Harvard study examined learning outcomes in a large physics course where students used a custom-designed AI chatbot tutor compared to traditional active learning instruction. Students in the AI-tutored group demonstrated approximately double the learning gains compared to the in-class group and reported significantly higher engagement and motivation. The researchers suggest AI tutoring is particularly effective for introducing challenging material outside of class, potentially freeing class time for higher-order skills development.
keyFindings: Learning gains for students in the AI-tutored group were about double those for students in the in-class group, based on pretest and posttest measures of content mastery.
Students using the AI tutor reported significantly more engagement, motivation to learn, enjoyment, and positive growth mindset compared to in-class instruction.

The AI tutor's ability to provide personalized feedback and allow self-pacing accommodated students with varying background knowledge levels, addressing engagement gaps present in traditional classrooms.

The custom AI tutor was built on the GPT API with research-based prompt engineering and pre-vetted conversations to ensure accuracy and well-structured scaffolding rather than default ChatGPT behavior.
methodology: Institutional Review Board-approved study conducted in fall 2023 with 194 students enrolled in Physical Sciences 2 (physics for life sciences majors) at Harvard. The experiment used a crossover design with two groups experiencing two consecutive weekly lessons in alternating conditions: Group 1 received instructor-guided active learning in week 1 and AI-supported home lessons in week 2, with Group 2 conditions reversed. Learning outcomes were measured using pretests and posttests to assess content mastery. Students also completed self-report questionnaires about engagement, enjoyment, motivation, and growth mindset. The AI tutor was custom-designed by lecturers Gregory Kestin and Kelly Miller with instructions crafted to emulate seasoned instruction.
qualifiers: Authors note the final study results are 'pending publication.' The analysis is described as 'preliminary study analysis.' Study was limited to one physics course at one institution. Researchers acknowledge potential for AI misuse in education and emphasize AI tutors should support rather than replace in-person instruction and should promote critical thinking rather than do the thinking for students. The researchers note this approach shows particular advantage 'when students are first being introduced to concepts and problems on topics that only some students have seen before.'
